title: .NET TLS server cannot use a TPM-backed private key on Ubuntu
body: I'm trying to implement the equivalent of an OpenSSL TLS server in a .NET Core library on Ubuntu, with the server certificate's private key stored in the TPM at a persistent handle. Windows abstracts TPM access through the certificate store, but Ubuntu does not. I tried adapting the SafeEvpPKeyHandle and RSAOpenSsl example from another runtime issue with the TPM handle, but it fails.

symptoms_visible: I cannot get my Ubuntu .NET TLS server to use the certificate private key stored at a persistent TPM handle, although this setup can be expressed with openssl s_server and the tpm2tss engine.
N0.label: N0 TPM-backed TLS server requested

symptoms_visible: On .NET 8, OpenPrivateKeyFromEngine first reports 'no such engine'. After selecting OpenSSL 1.1, it reaches the engine but reports 'ENGINE_load_private_key: failed loading private key'.
The OpenSSL command-line server can load the same TPM handle after I press Enter at its password prompt.
N1.label: N1 engine and environment evidence collected

symptoms_visible: With the patched .NET 8 native cryptography library, OpenPrivateKeyFromEngine no longer produces the previous engine key-loading error.
When I first use the resulting certificate with SslStream, it reports that m_safeCertContext is an invalid handle.
N2.label: N2 patched engine loading reaches TLS

symptoms_visible: After correcting my disposed-certificate mistake, the connection starts its handshake but fails with 'tlsv1 alert decrypt error'.
N3.label: N3 certificate lifetime fixed, handshake still fails

symptoms_visible: I can retrieve the certificate's RSA private key and generate a signature with it.
With the default TLS settings, openssl s_server using the same certificate and TPM handle also ends with a decrypt alert, while curl reports an RSA salt-length check failure.
N4.label: N4 TPM signing works and TLS failure reproduced outside .NET

symptoms_visible: OpenSSL successfully completes the TLS 1.2 connection when I select AES128-GCM-SHA256.
The .NET server still reports the decrypt alert after Client Key Exchange even when its cipher policy selects TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.
N5_x.label: N5_x matching cipher alone does not fix .NET handshake

symptoms_visible: When I make the .NET application use OpenSSL 1.1.1, the TPM-backed TLS server connects successfully.
N6.label: N6 patched build verified end to end

symptoms_visible: My locally patched .NET 8 build loads the TPM-backed RSA key and completes the TLS connection with the working OpenSSL 1.1.1 and TLS 1.2 configuration; I have not reported retesting an official serviced build.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix merged after local validation

question_patterns: What exact exception do you get from OpenPrivateKeyFromEngine?
What happens when you run the engine-loading code on the target machine?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On .NET 8, OpenPrivateKeyFromEngine("tpm2tss", "0x8100002") throws error:13000074:engine routines::no such engine.

question_patterns: Does the OpenSSL command-line utility see the engine?
What does the OpenSSL engine-listing command report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The command line reports '(tpm2tss) TPM2-TSS engine for OpenSSL', lists RSA and RAND, and says it is available.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The command-line utility also says there is no such engine.
The engine is available and lists RSA support, but not RAND.

question_patterns: Can you check which OpenSSL version .NET loaded and try selecting the older installed OpenSSL libraries?
If more than one OpenSSL version is installed, what error do you get after making .NET use the same generation as the command-line engine?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: After exporting CLR_OPENSSL_VERSION_OVERRIDE=1.1, the error changes to error:26096080:engine routines:ENGINE_load_private_key:failed loading private key.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Selecting OpenSSL 1.1 makes the key load successfully and the complete TLS connection work without any runtime patch.
The same private-key loading error occurs with an equivalent OpenSSL 1.1 library suffix.

question_patterns: Can the command-line TLS server load that exact TPM handle on the same machine?
What happens at the password or PIN prompt when the command-line server loads the key?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The command-line s_server loads the same handle. It prints 'Enter password for user key', I only press Enter, and then it reaches ACCEPT.

question_patterns: Please share the full output of dotnet --info from the target machine.
Which exact .NET runtime, Ubuntu release and architecture should a test build target?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The target is Ubuntu 22.04 x64 with Microsoft.NETCore.App 8.0.10. The host version is 8.0.10 and the RID is ubuntu.22.04-x64.

edges.comment: c1-c10 and c17-c19. These messages describe the reporter's target plus corroborating tests from participant2; the affected participants are folded into one simulated user side. The OpenSSL-version selection is a handler-initiated probe, so its raw error transition is modeled as clarification rather than a solution.

solution.intent: Change the .NET native OpenSSL interop so an ENGINE private-key load rejected with a null UI method is retried with a non-null, non-interactive UI method, then test that native library on the reporter's .NET 8 Ubuntu environment.
solution.concrete_example: Build the matching .NET 8 native cryptography library with the ENGINE key-loading change, replace libSystem.Security.Cryptography.Native.OpenSsl.so in the self-contained server, and rerun OpenPrivateKeyFromEngine against the TPM handle.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the differing .NET and command-line outcomes. Maintainers traced those outcomes through ENGINE_load_private_key and the tpm2tss source, determining that .NET passed NULL for UI_METHOD while the engine rejected NULL and the OpenSSL command line supplied a default UI method.

edges.comment: c13-c20 and c30. Maintainers identified the null UI_METHOD behavior and supplied instructions for building a patched .NET 8 native library. The reporter confirmed that this removed the original SafeEvpPKeyHandle engine-loading error.

solution.intent: Correct the application certificate lifetime so SslStream receives a valid, undisposed certificate and key while authentication is running.
solution.concrete_example: Keep the X509Certificate2 returned by GetCertificate alive through AuthenticateAsServer, and dispose the certificate and related key wrappers deterministically only after the TLS operation is finished.

edges.comment: c30-c32. A maintainer recognized the invalid-handle stack as a disposed certificate. The reporter corrected that application bug and reached the later TLS handshake failure.

question_patterns: Can you call GetRSAPrivateKey on the returned certificate and sign a small value directly?
Before debugging the TLS stream, please try a direct RSA SignData operation and report its output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The signature test works. I get a full hexadecimal RSA signature for empty data using SHA-256 and PKCS#1 padding.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The direct SignData call fails with the same TPM or private-key loading error.
The signature succeeds but produces a different hexadecimal signature value.

question_patterns: Can you run the command-line TLS server with the same certificate and TPM handle and then make a real request to it?
Does the full TLS exchange work outside .NET with the same certificate and key?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the same certificate and handle, openssl s_server reaches ACCEPT but the request ends with 'tlsv1 alert decrypt error'. Curl reports 'rsa routines::salt length check failed'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The OpenSSL server completes the TLS request successfully with its default settings, while only SslStream fails.

edges.comment: c37-c42. Direct signing and a full openssl s_server request were requested as measurements. The raw outputs show that primitive signing works and that the same TLS symptom can occur outside .NET; the conclusion that the handshake error is separate from the runtime ENGINE-loading defect remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Use a TLS 1.2 cipher suite compatible with the RSA certificate and map the OpenSSL cipher name to the correct IANA enum used by CipherSuitesPolicy.
solution.concrete_example: For OpenSSL's AES128-GCM-SHA256, use TlsCipherSuite.TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 in the .NET TLS 1.2 policy; preferably test the PFS-capable TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 alternative if the TPM supports it.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers mapped the OpenSSL name AES128-GCM-SHA256 to the IANA name TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and pointed out that TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 is a TLS 1.3 suite. The corrected cipher lets the OpenSSL test work but does not, by itself, resolve the reporter's .NET handshake.

edges.comment: c45-c50. The reporter first selected a TLS 1.3 enum while forcing TLS 1.2, then used the corrected TLS 1.2 RSA suite. OpenSSL succeeded, but .NET still failed after Client Key Exchange, so claiming the cipher correction alone fixes the .NET scenario is a known blind path.

question_patterns: Which OpenSSL library is the .NET process actually using for this final test, and what happens when you select the older installed library?
Please rerun the same .NET TLS test while binding the process to the OpenSSL version used by the working engine setup and report whether the handshake completes.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: When we set the .NET application to OpenSSL 1.1.1, it works correctly. The TPM-backed server completes the connection, so we are good with the runtime merge request.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same decrypt alert occurs with OpenSSL 1.1.1 and the matching TLS 1.2 cipher.
It also works with another compatible OpenSSL 1.1.1 patch build on the same Ubuntu release.

edges.comment: c50-c51. Selecting the OpenSSL library is a version/configuration probe and remains a clarification even though it also provides the working deployment configuration. The reporter supplies only the observed successful connection.

solution.intent: Ship the validated .NET OpenSSL ENGINE-loading change that retries with a non-null UI method, while retaining the engine-compatible OpenSSL and TLS 1.2 configuration validated for this TPM deployment.
solution.concrete_example: Use a .NET build containing the native ENGINE-loading retry, bind this engine-based deployment to OpenSSL 1.1.1, keep the certificate alive for the handshake, and select the matching TLS 1.2 RSA cipher policy. The backports were later merged, but the reporter did not post a retest of an official serviced build.
solution.inference_hint: The patched native library removing the original key-load failure validates the runtime fix. The later evidence—successful direct signing, the same decrypt alert in openssl s_server, cipher-dependent OpenSSL success, and final .NET success with the compatible OpenSSL library—shows that the handshake problem was a separate configuration and compatibility layer rather than evidence against the UI_METHOD fix.

edges.comment: c51-c54. The reporter validated the patched .NET 8 native library end to end in the working OpenSSL configuration. Maintainers later reported that the backports were merged, but the reporter did not retest an official serviced build, so the terminal state does not claim that verification.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the runtime defect: .NET passed a null UI_METHOD to ENGINE_load_private_key, while the TPM engine rejected a null UI method even for a key whose prompt accepted an empty response.

Must ground that diagnosis in the differing raw outcomes: the command-line engine could load the handle, selecting the matching OpenSSL generation moved .NET past engine discovery to private-key loading, and the patched native library removed that key-loading error.
Must use the non-null, non-interactive UI-method retry as the runtime fix; selecting a TLS cipher or changing certificate trust alone is not a fix for the original ENGINE key-loading failure.
Must not claim that the corrected TLS 1.2 cipher selection alone resolves the .NET server, because the reporter still saw the decrypt alert until the process used the compatible OpenSSL 1.1.1 setup.
Must distinguish the disposed-certificate error and later TLS handshake compatibility problem from the original runtime ENGINE-loading defect.
Must ask the reporter to verify an official build containing the fix before declaring the serviced release fully verified; only the locally patched build was confirmed end to end in the thread.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced application developer integrating .NET TLS with TPM-backed keys on Linux; comfortable with C#, OpenSSL commands, runtime environment variables, self-contained deployment, native library replacement, and packet captures, but relies on runtime maintainers for interop internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, collaborative, and test-driven; shares exact exceptions and commands, follows build and diagnostic instructions, and reports incremental progress while asking concise implementation questions.
